prompt: Put the stages a ride passes through at Roda Livre in order, from the dock to Marta.
hint: The lesson’s title lists them in this order.
trap: Reis and Housley list storage second, because data is stored where it is born; this course follows the order a ride is handled in.

prompt: What is wrong with picturing the lifecycle as a conveyor belt?
hint: Think about Monday, Tuesday and a re-run.

choices.text: It runs every day, it runs some days twice, and storage sits under every stage rather than in the row
choices.why: Right: three ways the belt misleads.

choices.text: A belt has five stations and the lifecycle has four of them
choices.why: The count is not the problem; the lifecycle has five stages.

choices.text: A belt moves too slowly to stand for data that arrives each night
choices.why: Speed is not what the picture gets wrong.

choices.text: Data moves right to left in a real pipeline, against the belt
choices.why: The direction is fine; the once-only, single pass is not.

prompt: Why does the lesson’s figure draw storage underneath the other stages instead of in the row?
hint: Which stages read or write a directory?

choices.text: Because it is the cheapest stage, and cheap things go at the bottom
choices.why: Cost has nothing to do with where it is drawn.

choices.text: Because it happens last, after delivery
choices.why: It happens throughout, not after.

choices.text: Because every other stage reads it or writes it
choices.why: Right: it is the floor under the others.

choices.text: Because the undercurrents include it
choices.why: Storage is a stage; the undercurrents are security, data management and the rest.

prompt: Which of these are undercurrents in Reis and Housley’s picture, rather than stages? Choose all that apply.
hint: They apply to every stage at once.

choices.text: Security
choices.why: Yes: who may read raw is a question at every stage.

choices.text: Orchestration
choices.why: Yes: what runs each program at 02:00.

choices.text: Ingestion
choices.why: No: a ride passes through ingestion; it is a stage.

choices.text: Data management
choices.why: Yes: what the columns mean, everywhere.

choices.text: Transformation
choices.why: No: it is the stage that cleans, joins and counts.

prompt: What do Reis and Housley call the stage this course calls delivery?
hint: It is one English word.

choices.text: Reporting
choices.why: A report is one form of delivery, not the stage’s name.

choices.text: Publishing
choices.why: Not their word for it.

choices.text: Consumption
choices.why: Not their word; it names the reader’s side.

choices.text: Serving
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Why does the app’s rides table hold a price but no count of rides per station?
hint: What was the app built to do?

choices.text: Counting per station would be too slow for a database to do
choices.why: A database counts quickly; it was simply never asked to.

choices.text: It was built to charge customers for rides, and a count per station charges nobody
choices.why: Right: it holds what charging needs, nothing a report alone would want.

choices.text: The LGPD forbids storing counts in an operational system
choices.why: A count is not personal data, and the law says nothing of the kind.

choices.text: The data team asked the app team to leave counts out
choices.why: Nobody asked; the shape comes from the app’s own job.

prompt: A customer changes their e-mail in the app. What happens to the old address in the app’s database?
hint: Operational systems keep the present.

choices.text: It moves to a history table the app keeps for analysts
choices.why: Nothing in the section says the app keeps history; it updates in place.

choices.text: It stays beside the new one, marked as old
choices.why: That is what a history would do, and the app is not one.

choices.text: It is overwritten by the new one, and the app keeps no record of what it was
choices.why: Right: unless a copy was taken first, it is gone.

choices.text: It is sent to the raw zone automatically
choices.why: Raw holds only what ingestion copied, when it copied it.

prompt: The app writes `started_at` as `2025-09-15 06:01`. What does every later reader need to know that the value does not say?
hint: Lesson 1 had a Wednesday with 27 hours.

choices.text: The time zone the app wrote it in
choices.why: Right: it is Curitiba’s clock, and nothing in the value says so.

choices.text: The second the ride started, which was rounded away
choices.why: Seconds would add precision, not meaning.

choices.text: Which bicycle it was, since the value alone cannot say
choices.why: That is in another column, `bike_id`.

choices.text: The date format, since it could be day-first
choices.why: The format is unambiguous here: year, month, day.

prompt: The dock sensors keep two days of readings. The nightly copy fails on Friday and nobody notices until Tuesday. What is lost?
hint: Count which days the sensors still hold on Tuesday.

choices.text: Nothing, since the next successful copy brings the missed days along
choices.why: The next copy can only take what the source still has.

choices.text: Friday’s readings and whatever else fell outside the two days
choices.why: Right: the first copy was the only history, and it was not taken.

choices.text: Only the copy’s log, which says it failed
choices.why: The log survives; the readings are what is gone.

choices.text: Tuesday’s readings, because the copy is a day behind
choices.why: Tuesday is still on the sensors’ server.

prompt: A row in the source looks wrong. What does ingestion do with it?
hint: The copy is the evidence.

choices.text: Fixes it on the way in, so that the warehouse receives clean rows from day one
choices.why: Fixing is a later stage’s job, done where it can be undone.

choices.text: Skips it and writes a warning to the log
choices.why: Skipping it changes the evidence of what the source said.

choices.text: Asks the app team to fix the source first
choices.why: Worth telling them, but the copy still takes what is there.

choices.text: Copies it as it is, and leaves the judging to a later stage
choices.why: Right: decide what is wrong later, on a copy.

prompt: Why does `ingest.py` open `app.db` with `mode=ro`?
hint: `ro` stands for two words.

choices.text: It makes the reading faster
choices.why: Speed is not the reason given.

choices.text: SQLite requires it when two programs share one file
choices.why: SQLite allows several readers without it.

choices.text: It returns rows as dictionaries
choices.why: That is `row_factory`, on the next line.

choices.text: So it cannot change the source
choices.why: Right: read-only, even by mistake.

prompt: Match each Roda Livre source to how its data reaches the data team.
hint: Who starts the copy, and how much does it take?

pairs.right: pulled, one day at a time

prompt: Why is the stations table copied whole every night while the rides table is copied one day at a time?
hint: Compare twelve rows with millions.

choices.text: Stations are personal data, so they must be refreshed daily
choices.why: Station names are not personal data.

choices.text: Twelve rows cost nothing to copy; millions do
choices.why: Right: full where it is cheap and never misses a change, incremental where it is not.

choices.text: Rides cannot be copied whole, because SQLite refuses large reads
choices.why: It would read them; it would just copy the same rides again and again.

choices.text: The app deletes old rides each night, so only a day is left
choices.why: The app keeps its rides; the copy chooses to take one day.

prompt: A ride that started on Monday is refunded on Wednesday, and the app sets its price to zero. What does the day-by-day ingestion of this lesson copy?
hint: Which day does `ingest.py` select, and by which column?

choices.text: The original price, and it misses the refund
choices.why: Right: not new by date, so missed. Lesson 7 is about that.

choices.text: The refund, in Wednesday’s partition, since the row changed then
choices.why: It selects by `started_at`, and the ride started on Monday.

choices.text: Both prices, side by side, in Monday’s partition
choices.why: A day is copied once; nothing goes back to add the new price.

choices.text: An error, because a row changed after it was copied
choices.why: Nothing notices; that is the trouble.

prompt: Which zone is the only one that cannot be rebuilt?
hint: The others are the output of programs.

choices.text: Curated, because people read it
choices.why: It is rebuilt from cleaned by running the transformation again.

choices.text: Cleaned, because its rules have changed since
choices.why: Changed rules are exactly why it gets rebuilt.

choices.text: Raw, a copy of what the source said that day
choices.why: Right: it is the output of a moment that has passed.

choices.text: None: every zone is the output of a program
choices.why: Raw is the output of a copy at a moment the source has moved past.

prompt: Marta decides a false start is under one minute, not two. With the raw zone kept, what is the fix?
hint: Which zone still holds the rides between one and two minutes?

choices.text: Edit the curated counts by hand for the past months
choices.why: Hand edits are how two numbers for one question begin.

choices.text: Ask the app for the dropped rides and add them to clean
choices.why: Raw already holds them; the app may have changed them since.

choices.text: Apply the new rule from today and leave the past as it is
choices.why: Then this week and last week count different things.

choices.text: Change the one number in the transformation and run it again over every day since the beginning
choices.why: Right: raw still holds every ride, so the zones come out as if the rule had always been one.

prompt: In the names Databricks made popular, the raw zone is called ___.
hint: The cheapest of the three metals.

prompt: What does the directory name `date=2025-09-15` make easy?
hint: It is called partitioning.

choices.text: Sorting the rides by time inside the file
choices.why: The directory says nothing about order inside a file.

choices.text: Finding or replacing one day alone
choices.why: Right: a tool skips the other days, and a re-run replaces one directory.

choices.text: Compressing the day so it takes less disk
choices.why: Compression is a format question, lesson 6.

choices.text: Spreading the day over several machines
choices.why: That is the larger meaning of the word, in lesson 9.

prompt: Which of these are rules for the raw zone? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three were listed.

choices.text: Ingestion is the one stage that writes to it
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: A row in it is never patched by hand
choices.why: Yes: a whole day is replaced by copying it again.

choices.text: It is kept for ever, whatever it holds
choices.why: No: as long as somebody may need to rebuild, and personal data is a reason not to keep it longer.

choices.text: Delivery reads from it directly
choices.why: No: delivery reads curated.

choices.text: It is kept as long as a rebuild needs it
choices.why: Yes.

prompt: Match each operation in `transform.py` to what it does there.
hint: Three operations, three lines of the program.

pairs.right: give each ride its station’s name

prompt: "A ride under 2 minutes is a false start." What kind of statement is that?
hint: Would a different number be wrong, or just different?

choices.text: A fact measured from the dock sensors
choices.why: The sensors measure docks; nobody measured where a false start ends.

choices.text: A limit imposed by SQLite’s integer type
choices.why: The type stores 0 and 1 happily.

choices.text: A decision Marta and the team made, written down in code
choices.why: Right: another threshold gives another report.

choices.text: A rule the app enforces before it writes the ride to its database
choices.why: The app writes rides of 0 and 1 minutes; the transformation drops them.

prompt: What is the difference between ETL and ELT?
hint: Look at where the T sits in each name.

choices.text: Where the T runs, and whether raw is kept
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: ELT transforms less, because the warehouse does the cleaning by itself
choices.why: Both transform the same amount.

choices.text: ETL is for files and ELT is for databases
choices.why: Both handle both.

choices.text: ETL is the older name for exactly the same process
choices.why: The order changed, and with it whether raw rows stay in the warehouse.

prompt: A company must not store customers’ phone numbers, but runs ELT for everything else. Where does the phone number go?
hint: In ELT, raw rows land in the warehouse first.

choices.text: Into the raw zone, to be deleted the next night
choices.why: Then it was stored, for a night, which is what was forbidden.

choices.text: It is removed by a transformation on the way in, before anything is stored
choices.why: Right: a transformation on the way in, which is ETL for that column.

choices.text: Into the curated zone, where analysts are trusted with it
choices.why: Curated is built from raw, so it was stored first.

choices.text: Into the warehouse, and hidden from every report
choices.why: Hidden is still stored.

prompt: Why does `transform.py` open its output files with `"w"`?
hint: What happens when it runs a second time?

choices.text: Because `"a"` is not allowed for CSV files
choices.why: Python appends to a CSV file without complaint.

choices.text: To make the files smaller than appending would
choices.why: The first run writes the same bytes either way.

choices.text: Because `"w"` checks the rows for duplicates as it writes
choices.why: It checks nothing; it empties the file first.

choices.text: So a second run writes the same files again
choices.why: Right: same raw in, same files out.

prompt: Match each form of delivery to who or what reads it at Roda Livre.
hint: Not every reader is a person.

prompt: What makes reverse ETL "reverse"?
hint: Compare its direction with ingestion’s.

choices.text: It reads the warehouse backwards, newest rows first
choices.why: Order of reading is not the point.

choices.text: It undoes a transformation that went wrong
choices.why: That would be a re-run from raw.

choices.text: It loads first and transforms afterwards
choices.why: That is ELT, a different reordering.

choices.text: Curated data goes back into an operational tool
choices.why: Right: the opposite direction to ingestion.

prompt: The dashboard counts rides from raw and the report counts them from curated. What does Marta see?
hint: What does curated leave out that raw has?

choices.text: The same number twice, so nothing is wrong
choices.why: Raw still holds the false starts.

choices.text: A bigger total on one screen than on the other, false starts and all
choices.why: Right: two numbers for one question.

choices.text: An error on the dashboard, because raw is not readable
choices.why: Raw is plain JSON Lines; it reads fine, and that is the trouble.

choices.text: A lower dashboard, because raw is a day behind
choices.why: Raw is written first, so it is never behind curated.

prompt: The data team changes the false-start rule and tells nobody. The report arrives on time. Which promise was broken?
hint: The report promises two things.

choices.text: That "rides" means what it meant last week
choices.why: Right: Marta compares two weeks and reads a difference the pipeline made up.

choices.text: None, because the report arrived by eight
choices.why: Being on time is only one of the two promises.

choices.text: Freshness, because the old rule is stale
choices.why: Freshness is about when it arrives.

choices.text: Privacy, because a rule about people changed
choices.why: The rule is about ride length, not about people.

prompt: How many rides did `ingest.py` copy for 2025-09-15?
hint: The first line it prints.

prompt: How many rides did `transform.py` drop as false starts on the first run?
hint: raw minus kept.

prompt: Which file does `report.py` read?
hint: Delivery reads one zone.

choices.text: `app.db`, to have the newest rides
choices.why: Delivery never asks the source.

choices.text: `raw/date=2025-09-15/rides.jsonl`
choices.why: Raw still has the false starts in it.

choices.text: `curated/date=2025-09-15/rides_per_station.csv`
choices.why: Right: the curated zone and nothing else.

choices.text: `clean/date=2025-09-15/rides.jsonl`
choices.why: Clean has rides; the report wants counts, which curated holds.

prompt: What makes this pipeline "readable" when the report looks wrong?
hint: Where does each stage write?

choices.text: The programs print a log line for each ride they handle
choices.why: They print one summary line each.

choices.text: Every program is written in one file of under ten lines
choices.why: They are under forty, and length is not the point.

choices.text: The report prints which stage produced each of its numbers
choices.why: It prints counts; tracing them is section 10’s job.

choices.text: Each stage’s output is a plain file on disk
choices.why: Right: "which stage?" has an answer in a text editor.

prompt: After `ingest.py` ran a second time, how many lines did `raw/date=2025-09-15/rides.jsonl` hold?
hint: `wc -l`.

prompt: A step that gives the same result however many times it runs is called ___.
hint: A long word from mathematics.

prompt: The second `ingest.py` run doubled the report. Which program was at fault?
hint: Which one added to a file instead of replacing it?

choices.text: `transform.py`, which counted every row it was given without checking for repeats
choices.why: It overwrote its output and counted faithfully what raw said.

choices.text: `ingest.py`, which opened raw with `"a"` and appended the day to itself
choices.why: Right: `"a"` appended Monday to Monday.

choices.text: `report.py`, which summed the counts
choices.why: It read a curated file that was already doubled.

choices.text: `app.py`, which generated the rides twice
choices.why: It ran once; the app had 187 rides that day throughout.

prompt: Why did the station names come out right even though `stations.jsonl` held every station twice?
hint: How does `transform.py` store the names?

choices.text: The second copy of each station was identical, so Python ignored it
choices.why: Python ignores nothing; the dictionary kept one value per key.

choices.text: `ingest.py` copies stations in full, which removes duplicates
choices.why: A full copy appended twice is two full copies.

choices.text: `transform.py` keeps the names in a dictionary, one per id
choices.why: Right, and by luck: a join keeping every match would have counted four times.

choices.text: The stations table has a primary key that refuses duplicates
choices.why: That key lives in `app.db`; the JSON file has no keys at all.

prompt: What makes `ingest_replace.py` idempotent?
hint: Two lines changed.

choices.text: It removes the day’s directory, creates it empty and writes each file with `"w"`
choices.why: Right: removed, recreated, written with `"w"`.

choices.text: It checks each ride id against the raw file before writing it
choices.why: That would be the unique-key approach; this one replaces the day.

choices.text: It runs faster, so a retry never overlaps the first run
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; the second run replaces the first.

choices.text: It reads the app’s database with `mode=ro`
choices.why: So did `ingest.py`, which doubled.

prompt: Put the layers in the order a trace walks them, starting from the number in the report.
hint: Backwards through the lifecycle.
trap: Lineage is the lifecycle read in the other direction.

prompt: How many rides from Rua XV on 2025-09-15 does the app’s database hold, according to `trace.py`?
hint: The bottom line of the counts.

prompt: The app team wants to rename `start_station`. Which use of lineage answers what that breaks?
hint: Read the path forwards.

choices.text: Trust, because it lets Marta defend the number in a meeting
choices.why: Trust reads the path backwards from one number.

choices.text: Impact: the path read forwards from the column
choices.why: Right: from the source column forwards to every table and report.

choices.text: Erasure, because it lists every zone a customer reached
choices.why: Erasure follows a person’s rows, not a column.

choices.text: Freshness, because the rename delays the next copy
choices.why: Freshness is a promise about time, not a use of lineage.

prompt: Caio wants rides per station per hour for his model. Which zone should he read?
hint: Every form of delivery reads the same zone.

choices.text: Raw, so that no rule hides anything from the model
choices.why: Then his model counts false starts and the report does not.

choices.text: The app’s database, which has the freshest rides
choices.why: Reading the source for analysis is what ingestion exists to avoid.

choices.text: Cleaned, and he aggregates the rows himself
choices.why: Then his per-hour count is a second definition in a notebook.

choices.text: Curated, in a feature table built for his model from the same definitions as the report
choices.why: Right: a feature table is one more curated table.

prompt: A bug in `transform.py` is found three months after it shipped. What does the fix cost, with raw kept?
hint: Which zones are the output of a program?

choices.text: Re-ingesting three months from the app, which may have changed them
choices.why: Raw already holds them as they were; the app holds them as they are now.

choices.text: Accept three wrong months and fix it from today
choices.why: That is the cost without raw.

choices.text: Edit the curated files for those months by hand
choices.why: A program wrote them; a program rewrites them.

choices.text: Fix the code and re-run it over those days
choices.why: Right: cleaned and curated come out as though the bug never existed.

prompt: A nightly job fails at 02:00, and the scheduler retries it at 02:30. What has to be true for the retry to be safe?
hint: Did the first try write anything before it failed?

choices.text: The job finishes in under thirty minutes
choices.why: Duration is not what makes a second run harmless.

choices.text: The job gives the same result run twice
choices.why: Right: the retry replaces whatever the first try left.

choices.text: The first try wrote nothing at all before failing
choices.why: Nobody can promise that; idempotence makes it not matter.

choices.text: The source has not changed between the two tries
choices.why: A replaced day simply takes the newer state; that is not the danger.

prompt: In `ingest.py`, the mode that adds to an existing file is `"___"`.
hint: Compare it with the mode `ingest_replace.py` uses.

prompt: Put the four programs of `~/roda/lifecycle` in the order the pipeline runs them.
hint: Each reads what the one before it wrote.
trap: `trace.py` is not in the pipeline: it reads every layer after the fact.
